task.description:
WF-03 Step 3 IDIOM/DESIGN-INTEGRITY GATE for ISS-0426. SECURITY-REVIEWER has already PASSED (handoff step-03b): no INV violation, production semantics confirmed untouched (113 insertions / 0 deletions in executor.ex), the two public @doc false seams judged an acceptable availability-only risk with no production call path, and the test tagging confirmed to still execute (37 passed + 11 excluded default; 11 passed + 37 excluded isolated). Do not re-run the security scope test -- review for YOUR scope: idiomatic OTP usage, supervision integrity, scope creep, and decision-record consistency.

WHAT TO REVIEW, run-specifically:

1. OTP IDIOM OF THE SECOND SEAM. run_with_heap_limit_sync/4 uses :erlang.spawn_opt/2 with a monitor and a bare `receive` that has NO `after` clause -- an unbounded receive. Judge this as OTP code. It deliberately mirrors the existing run_with_heap_limit/5's shape (which does have an `after`), so the question is not 'is spawn_opt idiomatic here' -- that pattern is already established in this module for a reason (max_heap_size is a spawn_opt). The question is whether an unbounded receive is acceptable in this codebase's idiom for a test-only helper, whether the three receive clauses are exhaustive over the monitored process's termination modes, and whether Process.demonitor/2 hygiene is correct on every path (a leaked monitor or a stray :DOWN left in the caller's mailbox is a real defect in a function tests call repeatedly).

2. DUPLICATION VS. THE ORIGINAL. The new seam is close to a copy of run_with_heap_limit/5 minus the `after` clause, and run_lua_wallclock_race_tests/0 in letflow.check.test.ex is described by ELIXIR-DEV as a 3-substitution copy of run_wasm_hang_tests/0. Both duplications were deliberate design decisions (letflow.check.test.ex is shared with the live concurrent run WF03-ISS0418-20260902, so additive-only was REQUIRED -- zero existing lines touched, which ORCH verified: 37 insertions / 0 deletions). Judge whether the duplication is justified or whether an extraction is warranted -- but weigh the concurrent-run constraint, which is real and which ORCH will rely on when sequencing the merge against ISS-0418. If you would normally demand a refactor here, say whether it should be deferred to a follow-up issue rather than done now.

3. SCOPE CREEP. The change should be: two additive seams, repointed Group 1 call sites, a new @tag on 11 tests, test_helper.exs exclusion wiring, and an additive check.test.ex subprocess. Confirm nothing else rode along. `git diff main...HEAD --stat` is your starting point.

4. DECISION-RECORD CONSISTENCY. Check the change against docs/migration/decisions/0014-scripting-plugin-runtime-strategy.md and REQ-155/156/162's own design docs -- particularly that nothing here silently re-decides the scripting runtime's timeout/security posture. The design doc lib/letflow/design/iss426-wallclock-test-contention.md is gate-approved; verify the IMPLEMENTATION matches what that design specifies rather than diverging from it (especially design sections 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.1.2a, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4).

5. THE CONTRACT COMMENT. Design section 2.1.2a's usage contract had to land in the seam's own @doc false/comment block -- the design gate FAILED TWICE on this exact point before passing. It is present at executor.ex:601-612 (ORCH verified). Judge whether it is written well enough to actually bind a future caller who reads only the source: does it state the rule, the reason, and the failure mode?

6. AN INCIDENTAL FINDING ELIXIR-DEV FLAGGED FOR YOU. The type checker now emits a non-fatal 'clause will never match' note at executor_test.exs:464 for a `refute match?({:error, {:wallclock_timeout, _}}, result)` line, because run_script_sync/3's narrower @spec correctly excludes wallclock_timeout as categorically unreachable. ELIXIR-DEV left it as-is (touching test assertions is TEST-DESIGNER's scope, not its own) and notes it fails nothing. Rule on it: is leaving a permanent 'will never match' warning in the tree acceptable, should the assertion be removed/rewritten by TEST-DESIGNER at Step 4, or is the warning itself valuable as a standing proof that the unreachability claim holds? State your preference clearly enough that ORCH can put it in TEST-DESIGNER's handoff.

You may READ anything. Do not edit lib/ or test/. Complete the handoff with a clear PASS/FAIL, per-item verdicts, and an explicit ruling on item 6; commit it to branch feature/WF03-ISS0426-20260902.

result.summary:
IDIOM/DESIGN-INTEGRITY GATE for ISS-0426: PASS. Re-derived every factual claim independently rather than accepting ELIXIR-DEV's/SECURITY-REVIEWER's reports (per HANDOFF_PROTOCOL S1.1). git diff main...HEAD --numstat confirms executor.ex 113/0, check.test.ex 37/0 -- matches ORCH's figures exactly, zero deletions in either file. mix compile --warnings-as-errors clean. mix test test/letflow/engine/lua/executor_test.exs -> 'Finished in 0.8 seconds / Result: 37 passed, 11 excluded' (ran fresh, this session). mix test --only lua_wallclock_race test/letflow/engine/lua/executor_test.exs -> 'Finished in 3.7 seconds / Result: 11 passed, 37 excluded' (ran fresh, this session) -- complementary counts, 37+11=48 matching baseline. grep counts: 11 @tag :lua_wallclock_race, 11 run_script_sync( call sites, 3 run_with_heap_limit_sync( call sites -- all match the design's S2.1 table (11 nil-heap, 3 heap-limited) and prior handoffs' claims.

ITEM 1 (OTP idiom of the second seam) -- ACCEPTABLE, no defect. Read run_with_heap_limit_sync/4 (executor.ex:601-660) directly against its sibling run_with_heap_limit/5 (executor.ex:541-584). The three receive clauses are exhaustive over every termination mode a :monitor can signal for this spawned process: (a) {^reply_ref, result} -- normal completion; (b) {:DOWN, ^monitor_ref, :process, ^pid, :killed} -- BEAM max_heap_size kill; (c) {:DOWN, ^monitor_ref, :process, ^pid, reason} -- catch-all for any other exit reason (crash, an unexpected early exit, etc). There is no fourth termination mode a process monitor can produce beyond a :DOWN with some reason or the process's own message arriving first -- :noproc cannot occur here because monitor and spawn happen atomically via :erlang.spawn_opt(fn, [:monitor, ...]), so the monitor is always installed before the process could exit. Demonitor hygiene is correct on every path and matches the established pattern exactly: clause (a) calls Process.demonitor(monitor_ref, [:flush]) before returning, exactly mirroring run_with_heap_limit/5's own clause (a). Clauses (b) and (c) call no explicit demonitor -- also correct and also matching the sibling function's own established pattern: a :DOWN message is only ever delivered once a monitor has already fired and the runtime has already torn it down, so there is nothing left to demonitor and no stray :DOWN can follow. This is not a gap introduced by removing the after clause -- it is the same hygiene the precedented function already has on its shared three clauses; the new function does not need an after-side demonitor because it has no after-side kill to demonitor after (unlike run_with_heap_limit/5, which demonitors implicitly by consuming the :DOWN its own Process.exit provokes inside the after branch's nested receive). No leaked monitor, no stray :DOWN left in the caller's mailbox on any of the three reachable paths.

On the broader idiom question -- is an unbounded receive with no after acceptable in this codebase for a test-only helper: YES, and it is the correct choice here, not merely tolerated. This is not a case of a missed after clause -- S2.1.2/2.1.2a of the design is a reasoned, gate-approved (after two rework cycles specifically on this point) decision that the safety property must live in a caller-discipline contract rather than a mechanism, because the mechanism this function exists to bypass (the wall-clock after kill) is exactly the thing under test in the tests that must NOT call this seam. Removing the after clause is the fix, not a shortcut around one. The residual risk (a hung ExUnit process) is bounded by ExUnit's own 60s default test timeout -- an external backstop this function correctly does not need to duplicate, since it has a closed, enumerable, 3-call-site caller set entirely inside one test file, not an open production caller set. The :erlang.spawn_opt/2 + monitor pattern itself is already this module's idiom for max_heap_size (spawn_opt is the only way to attach that option), so no new primitive is introduced -- only an existing primitive's after branch is a no-op by omission, which is a smaller and more legible change than inventing a different bypass mechanism would have been.

ITEM 2 (duplication vs. the original) -- JUSTIFIED AS-IS, no extraction, no deferral needed. run_with_heap_limit_sync/4 duplicates run_with_heap_limit/5's spawn_opt/monitor/receive shape minus the after clause; run_lua_wallclock_race_tests/0 duplicates run_wasm_hang_tests/0's shape with three substitutions. Independently confirmed the check.test.ex constraint the handoff states: git diff main...HEAD --numstat shows 37/0 for that file -- purely additive, zero existing lines touched, reconfirming ORCH's own measurement. Given that constraint is real (a live concurrent run, WF03-ISS0418-20260902, owns that file), an extraction that touched run_wasm_hang_tests/0 to share logic with the new function would violate the additive-only requirement outright -- there is no version of 'extract a shared helper' that doesn't edit the existing function's own lines or introduce a third abstraction layer neither run asked for. This is a case where duplication is the correct call, not a compromise: introducing a parameterized helper for two call sites, one of which cannot be touched, is scope creep in the wrong direction -- adding machinery to avoid four lines of repetition in a merge-fragile file. For executor.ex's own duplication (the two receive-block siblings), the precedent is even stronger: run_with_heap_limit/5's after branch is the one place the two functions genuinely differ in behavior, and a shared-body-with-a-flag design (e.g. an unbounded? argument) would obscure exactly the categorical/contractual distinction S2.1.1b's own contrast table exists to make legible -- collapsing the two into one parameterized function would make the weaker, contractual guarantee harder to see at the call site, which is a real idiom cost, not just a style preference. Given both duplications are small (under 20 lines each), have a stated and sound reason, and one is under a hard external constraint, no follow-up issue is warranted -- this is not the second-place-reached-for-a-crutch pattern worth flagging for future watching; it is the same shape reused because the shape itself needs to differ narrowly, which is what a well-placed sibling function is for.

ITEM 3 (scope creep) -- CLEAN. git diff main...HEAD --name-only lists exactly the 4 code/test files the task named (executor.ex, executor_test.exs, test_helper.exs, check.test.ex) plus expected bookkeeping (design doc, issue yaml, handoffs/, registry.json) -- no wasm files, no other lib/ module, no config file. Confirmed no supervision-tree change: no new Letflow.InstanceSupervisor-managed process, no new GenServer/gen_statem, no spawn outside the existing spawn_opt idiom already used by the sibling it mirrors. Both new functions are additive siblings of existing functions, not new abstractions, behaviours, or macros -- no framework machinery introduced ahead of what this fix needs.

ITEM 4 (decision-record consistency) -- CONSISTENT, no re-decision. Checked against docs/migration/decisions/0014-scripting-plugin-runtime-strategy.md's LUA-08/LUA-10 restatement (lines 432-439): both layers are mandatory -- :max_instructions for LUA-08, and an out-of-band supervising-process kill for LUA-10, and a test must confirm a script that traps its own instruction error is still terminated by the outer kill. This is exactly the categorical (S2.1.1b) vs contractual (S2.1.2a) distinction the design and implementation preserve: run_script_sync/3 still runs under Sandbox.new(max_instructions: budget) -- LUA-08's layer is untouched -- and neither seam changes what run_with_heap_limit/5's own after clause (LUA-10's host kill) does in production; the seams only remove a TEST CALLER's own patience for observing that kill, in call sites that were never asserting on it. config/config.exs:17's production lua_wallclock_timeout_ms (5_000) has an empty diff (confirmed by direct read, matches SECURITY-REVIEWER's finding). Nothing here silently weakens or reinterprets the two-layer LUA-08/LUA-10 posture 0014 restates, or REQ-155/156/162's own acceptance criteria -- the design's own S3 hard-constraint table maps directly onto 0014's restatement and the implementation matches the design.

ITEM 5 (the contract comment) -- WELL WRITTEN, binds a future caller who reads only the source. Read executor.ex:586-660 directly (the design's own line pointer, 601-612, is close but the landed comment block runs 586-624 in the final file with the binding contract text at approximately 601-621 after the two prior seams shifted line numbers slightly -- confirmed the actual content, not just the line range). It states: the RULE (callers must pass a workload that terminates independently of wall-clock enforcement -- either via :max_instructions alone with no pcall-trap-and-continue construct, or via a heap limit expected to trip), the REASON (removing the after clause is deliberate -- it is this seam's entire purpose, to let Group-1 tests assert an outcome without racing the production kill), and the FAILURE MODE (nothing will terminate a violating workload; the calling test process hangs until ExUnit's own default 60s timeout, described in-source as a materially worse failure mode than the flake this function exists to remove). It also correctly cross-references the categorical/contractual distinction against its sibling seam, so a reader choosing between the two functions for a new test is pointed at the right question (which guarantee does my workload actually need) rather than left to guess. This clears the bar the gate failed twice on -- it is substantive binding text at the call site, not a pointer back to a design doc nobody reads while writing a new test.

ITEM 6 (the executor_test.exs 'clause will never match' note) -- RULING: ACCEPTABLE AS-IS, do not rewrite at Step 4. Independently reproduced the warning (not merely accepted ELIXIR-DEV's claim): mix test test/letflow/engine/lua/executor_test.exs --only lua_wallclock_race emits 'warning: the following clause will never match: {:error, {:wallclock_timeout, _}} -> ... type warning found at: test/letflow/engine/lua/executor_test.exs:466 ... refute match?({:error, {:wallclock_timeout, _}}, result)' -- confirmed non-fatal: the test still passes (11 passed in that run), and confirmed it does NOT gate CI: mix compile --warnings-as-errors --force (the step CI's mix.exs alias actually runs) is clean, because that step compiles lib/, not test/ -- the type checker's test-file pass is a mix-test-only warning, invisible to the warnings-as-errors gate.

This is not a stale or misleading assertion left behind by an oversight -- it is a directly predicted consequence of S2.1.1b's own categorical-guarantee argument, now confirmed true by the type checker rather than merely asserted by the design doc. The assertion refute match?({:error, {:wallclock_timeout, _}}, result) was written when this test raced the real wall-clock kill (pre-fix) and was a legitimate, reachable negative assertion then. After routing through run_script_sync/3, whose @spec (executor.ex:518-523) correctly omits {:error, {:wallclock_timeout, _}} from its return-type union -- because that outcome is categorically unreachable through run_script/3's call chain, not merely absent from today's test inputs -- the type checker is doing exactly its job: proving, independently of any test run, that the seam's own hard constraint (S2.1.1b's categorical bound) actually holds at the type level. My preference, stated plainly for TEST-DESIGNER's handoff: leave the assertion and the warning in place. It is a standing, machine-checked proof that the unreachability claim central to this entire design (S2.1.1b, S4's 'structurally verifiable, not statistically' framing) continues to hold as the code evolves -- if a future change to run_script_sync/3's @spec or body ever reintroduced a path to {:error, {:wallclock_timeout, _}}, this exact warning would SILENTLY DISAPPEAR (the clause would become reachable again), which is a strictly worse signal than the warning's continued presence. Removing the assertion to silence the warning would delete that tripwire for no benefit -- the assertion costs nothing (it doesn't fail, it doesn't slow the suite, it isn't visible outside a raw mix test transcript), and CI does not see it. Rewriting it into some other assertion shape would either (a) assert something weaker and less informative, or (b) require dropping the very claim (this branch is impossible) that the categorical-guarantee argument exists to let a reader verify. TEST-DESIGNER should leave this specific assertion untouched at Step 4 and, if it adds new tests against run_script_sync/3, should not add a matching refute for the same now-unreachable shape elsewhere (same reasoning, no new instances) -- but should not spend effort removing or restructuring the one that already exists here.
result.next_action: PASS. Route to TEST-DESIGNER (Step 4). Ruling on item 6 for TEST-DESIGNER's handoff: leave test/letflow/engine/lua/executor_test.exs:466's refute match?({:error, {:wallclock_timeout, _}}, result) assertion as-is -- do not remove or rewrite it. The 'clause will never match' type-checker note it produces under mix test is a non-fatal, CI-invisible (mix compile --warnings-as-errors only checks lib/, not test/) warning that is in fact a standing, machine-verified proof that run_script_sync/3's categorical unreachability guarantee (design S2.1.1b) continues to hold. Do not add further assertions of this same now-unreachable shape against run_script_sync/3 elsewhere, but preserve this one.
